{{Short description|Logical fallacy}}
{{Distinguish|Paradox of the stone}}
{{original research|date=June 2025}}
<!--No citations are required in the article lead per [[MOS:LEADCITE]], as long as the content is cited in the article body, as it should be. Do not add missing-citation tags like {{cn}} to the lead. If necessary, {{not verified in body}} can be used, or the content removed.-->
'''Appeal to the stone''', also known as '''argumentum ad lapidem''', is a logical [[fallacy]] that dismisses an argument as untrue or absurd. The dismissal is made by stating or reiterating that the argument is absurd, without providing further argumentation. This theory is closely tied to [[proof by assertion]] due to the lack of evidence behind the statement and its attempt to persuade without providing any evidence.

Appeal to the stone is a [[Fallacy|logical fallacy]]. Specifically, it is an [[Fallacy#Informal fallacy|informal fallacy]], which means that it relies on [[inductive reasoning]] in an argument to justify an [[Proof by assertion|assertion]]. Informal fallacies contain erroneous reasoning in content of the argument and not the form or structure of it, as opposed to [[Fallacy#Formal fallacy|formal fallacies]], which contain erroneous reasoning in argument form.

==History==

===Origin===
[[File:Samuel Johnson (1911) Frontispiece.png|alt=Photograph of Dr.Samuel Johnson.|thumb|upright|[[Dr. Samuel Johnson]], originator of the appeal to the stone]]
The name "appeal to the stone" originates from an argument between [[Samuel Johnson|Dr. Samuel Johnson]] and [[James Boswell]] over [[George Berkeley]]'s theory of [[subjective idealism]] (known previously as "immaterialism").  Subjective idealism states that reality is dependent on a person's perceptions of the world and that material objects are intertwined with one's perceptions of these material objects.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Subjective idealism {{!}} philosophy|url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/subjective-idealism|access-date=2020-11-03|website=Encyclopedia Britannica|language=en|archive-date=7 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190607172044/https://www.britannica.com/topic/subjective-idealism|url-status=live}}</ref>

{{Blockquote|text=After we came out of the church, we stood talking for some time together of Bishop Berkeley's ingenious sophistry to prove the non-existence of matter, and that every thing in the universe is merely ideal. I observed, that though we are satisfied his doctrine is not true, it is impossible to refute it. I never shall forget the alacrity with which Johnson answered, striking his foot with mighty force against a large stone, till he rebounded from it, "I refute it ''thus''."<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Patey|first=Douglas Lane|date=January 1986|title=Johnson's Refutation of Berkeley: Kicking the Stone Again|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2709600|journal=Journal of the History of Ideas|volume=47|issue=1|pages=139–145|doi=10.2307/2709600|jstor=2709600|access-date=3 November 2020|archive-date=10 March 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210310205335/https://www.jstor.org/stable/2709600|url-status=live|url-access=subscription}}</ref>|author=James Boswell|title=''[[The Life of Samuel Johnson]]''}}

Johnson's intent, apparently,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Hallett|first=H. F.|year=1947|title=Dr. Johnson's Refutation of Bishop Berkeley|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2250515|journal=Mind|volume=56|issue=222|pages=132–147|doi=10.1093/mind/LVI.222.132|jstor=2250515|pmid=20243642|issn=0026-4423|access-date=3 November 2020|archive-date=29 August 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230829140451/https://www.jstor.org/stable/2250515|url-status=live|url-access=subscription}}</ref> was to imply that it was absurd of Berkeley to call such a stone "immaterial," when in fact Johnson could kick it with his foot. Others, however, have defended Johnson for making a valid and subtler philosophical point than is often realized.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Silver |first1=Bruce |title=Boswell on Johnson's Refutation of Berkeley: Revisiting the Stone |journal=Journal of the History of Ideas |date=July 1993 |volume=54 |issue=3 |pages=437–448 |url= http://www.jstor.org/stable/2710022 |access-date=29 April 2026}}</ref>

==Classification==
{{original research section|date=April 2025}}

===Informal logical fallacies===
{{off topic|date=May 2025}}
Informal logical fallacies are misconceptions derived from faulty reasoning. Informal logical fallacies use [[inductive reasoning]] and thus can cause errors in reasoning by creating the illusion of a sound argument when it is not sound.<ref>{{Cite book|url=http://ebooks.cambridge.org/ref/id/CBO9781139057509|title=The Cambridge Dictionary of Philosophy|date=2015|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-1-139-05750-9|editor-last=Audi|editor-first=Robert|edition=3|location=New York|doi=10.1017/cbo9781139057509}}</ref>

===Fallacy of irrelevance===
[[Irrelevant conclusion]]s, also known as ''ignoratio elenchi'' (Latin for "ignoring the list" or "ignoring refutation") or missing the point, follows a similar structure to appeal to the stone.{{citation needed|date=May 2025}}  As an informal fallacy, it may not be valid or sound in its reasoning.<ref>{{Citation|chapter=Whately and the study of fallacious reasoning|date=2016-12-05|chapter-url=http://dx.doi.org/10.4324/9781315253329-14|title=Historical Foundations of Informal Logic|pages=109–123|publisher=Routledge|doi=10.4324/9781315253329-14|isbn=978-1-315-25332-9|access-date=2020-11-19|archive-date=7 October 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231007222652/https://www.taylorfrancis.com/chapters/mono/10.4324/9781315253329-14/whately-study-fallacious-reasoning-douglas-walton-alan-brinton|url-status=live|chapter-url-access=subscription}}</ref> {{failed verification span|Irrelevant conclusions hold similarity to appeal to the stone because|date=May 2025}} it provides evidence towards a conclusion that has already been formed about the subject matter being debated, instead of the original subject that was being discussed.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=McNair|first1=G. H.|last2=Davies|first2=Arthur Ernest|date=1917-02-15|title=A Text-book on Logic|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.2307/2012956|journal=The Journal of Philosophy, Psychology and Scientific Methods|volume=14|issue=4|pages=109|doi=10.2307/2012956|jstor=2012956|s2cid=60139391|issn=0160-9335|access-date=19 November 2020 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> Dr. Samuel Johnson’s refutation of Bishop Berkeley’s theory of immaterialism by kicking a stone did not actually address the theory, but rather asserted a conclusion incompatible with the theory and then echoed his conclusion without discussing the subject matter of the theory of immaterialism directly.{{citation needed|date=May 2025}}

===Inductive reasoning===
Appeal to the stone utilizes inductive reasoning to derive its argument.{{citation needed|date=May 2025}} Formal fallacies use deductive reasoning and formal properties to structure an argument and inductive arguments do not use this structure. Inductive reasoning is reasoning with uncertain conclusions because of inferences made about a specific situation, object, or event.<ref>{{Cite book|date=2001-01-01|editor-last=Feeney|editor-first=Aidan|editor2-last=Heit|editor2-first=Evan|title=Inductive Reasoning|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1017/cbo9780511619304|doi=10.1017/cbo9780511619304|isbn=9780521856485|access-date=19 November 2020|archive-date=7 October 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231007222653/https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/inductive-reasoning/2AB7BDB17D918C482E0788A654BA26A2|url-status=live}}</ref> {{failed verification span|In the context of Appeal to the stone, inductive reasoning is asserted against an initial claim without further elaboration.|date=May 2025}} Inductive arguments can be affected by the acquisition of new information or evidence that can debunk an inductive assumption.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Deductive and Inductive Arguments {{!}} Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy|url=https://iep.utm.edu/ded-ind/|access-date=2020-11-19|language=en-US|archive-date=28 May 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100528032124/https://iep.utm.edu/ded-ind/|url-status=dead}}</ref>{{relevance inline|date=May 2025}}

Inductive reasoning asserts that the probability of a conclusion being correct is adequate evidence to support the argument.{{Citation needed | date = December 2023 }} Inductive arguments are judged on the strength or weakness of an argument and an argument's strength is subjective to each participant based on preconceptions about the subject being discussed.{{relevance inline|date=May 2025}}

The weakness of inductive reasoning (in comparison to [[deductive reasoning]]) lies in the inability to gauge the [[Validity (logic)|validity]] or [[soundness]] of claims within an argument. Validity of an argument is based on whether the information presented is factual. However, if evidence presented to prove a conclusion are false, this can provide a valid argument based on false information to substantiate the conclusion. Therefore, soundness of an argument is deemed when the assumptions of an argument are factual. Unlike deductive reasoning, inductive arguments cannot prove their deductive validity and therefore lead to the problem of induction.{{relevance inline|date=May 2025}}

==Structure of arguments==
{{original research section|date=April 2025}}
Arguments are typically structured by a claim being defended with reasoning and evidence. It typically consists of statements that provide premises to support a conclusion. In the case of appeal to the stone, there is an explicit conclusion but it is likely not substantiated with many premises to validate the conclusion being asserted.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Eemeren, F. H. van (Frans Hendrik), 1946-|title=A systematic theory of argumentation : the pragma-dialectical approach|date=2004|publisher=Cambridge University Press|others=Grootendorst, R. (Robert), 1944-2000.|isbn=0-511-16600-1|location=New York|oclc=69139196}}</ref>{{failed verification|date=May 2025}}

According to the theory of argumentation, there must be assumptions or premises that follow a method of reasoning or deduction to form the conclusion or point. An appeal to the stone's lack of evidence to substantiate the rejection of the initial claim puts the burden of proof on the other member of the argument and limits rebuttals.{{citation needed|date=May 2025}}

== Criticisms ==
{{original research section|date=April 2025}}

===Restricted debate===
In contrast to the [[burden of proof (philosophy)|burden of proof]], appeal to the stone does not allow for debate past the dismissal of the first claim. Therefore, the burden of proof is placed upon the person who made the initial statement to prove it is correct. However, when appeal to the stone is used to argue, there is a diminished ability for a person to create a rebuttal due to lack of elaboration on why there has been a disagreement.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hannibal|first1=Martin|last2=Mountford|first2=Lisa|date=September 2017|title=15. The Burden of Proof|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1093/he/9780198787679.003.0015|journal=Law Trove|doi=10.1093/he/9780198787679.003.0015|doi-broken-date=1 July 2025 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>{{failed verification|date=May 2025}} Additionally, the appeal to the stone technique is often paired with other logical fallacies that restrict the ability to further dialogue.<ref>{{Citation|title=HOW TO WIN AN ARGUMENT|date=2017-10-31|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.2307/j.ctvc77chr.5|pages=1–134|publisher=Princeton University Press|doi=10.2307/j.ctvc77chr.5|isbn=978-1-4008-8335-6|access-date=2020-11-19|archive-date=7 October 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231007222654/https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctvc77chr?turn_away=true|url-status=live|url-access=subscription}}</ref>{{failed verification|date=May 2025}} Participants presenting an appeal to the stone argument may use ad-hominem attacks<ref>{{Cite web|title=Definition of AD HOMINEM|url=https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/ad+hominem|access-date=2020-11-19|website=www.merriam-webster.com|language=en|archive-date=4 November 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161104174643/http://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/ad+hominem|url-status=live}}</ref>{{failed verification|date=May 2025}} to avoid the topic of discussion, or may pair it with a straw-man argument to discredit the other participant.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Definition of STRAW MAN|url=https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/straw+man|access-date=2020-11-19|website=www.merriam-webster.com|language=en|archive-date=25 June 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160625235048/http://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/straw+man|url-status=live}}</ref>{{failed verification|date=May 2025}}

===Two systems theory===
{{off topic|date=May 2025}}
The two systems theory, by Israeli psychologist [[Daniel Kahneman]] in his book ''[[Thinking, Fast and Slow]]'', explains the reasoning behind illogical fallacies. In the two systems theory, [[decision-making]] is categorized into system 1 and system 2. System 1 decision-making only uses quick and usually [[Heuristics in judgment and decision making|heuristic]] based interpretations to aid in low-engagement decisions. System 2 decision-making uses more deliberate and rational consideration when creating a conclusion.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Arvai|first=Joseph|date=November 2013|title=Thinking, fast and slow, Daniel Kahneman, Farrar, Straus & Giroux|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/13669877.2013.766389|journal=Journal of Risk Research|volume=16|issue=10|pages=1322–1324|doi=10.1080/13669877.2013.766389|s2cid=144799829|issn=1366-9877|access-date=3 November 2020|archive-date=7 October 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231007222654/https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/13669877.2013.766389|url-status=live|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Many illogical fallacies employ quick judgement based on emotion to create conclusions in system 1 type decision-making. However, by having a skeptical mindset on one’s own conclusions and engaging in methodological thinking, one can avoid an illogical fallacy.<ref>{{Citation|last1=Risen|first1=Jane|chapter=Informal Logical Fallacies|date=2006|chapter-url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/CBO9780511804632A016/type/book_part|title=Critical Thinking in Psychology|pages=110–130|editor-last=Sternberg|editor-first=Robert J.|place=Cambridge|publisher=Cambridge University Press|doi=10.1017/cbo9780511804632.008|isbn=978-0-511-80463-2|access-date=2020-11-03|last2=Gilovich|first2=Thomas|editor2-last=Roediger III|editor2-first=Henry L.|editor3-last=Halpern|editor3-first=Diane F.|archive-date=7 October 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231007222657/https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/critical-thinking-in-psychology/informal-logical-fallacies/AC3A27B92D8F5B7AB98BFD05E9158509|url-status=live|chapter-url-access=subscription}}</ref>

===Toulmin's argumentation framework===
[[File:Toulmin Argumentation Example.gif|alt=Toulmin argumentation framework example involving a claim, grounds, warrant, qualifier, rebuttal, and backing.|thumb|373x373px|Toulmin argumentation framework example]]
As demonstrated in [[Toulmin map|Toulmin’s argumentation framework]], the grounds of an assumption require warrant and backing to legitimize the claim and prove the soundness of the conclusion. The framework involves a claim, grounds, warrant, [[Grammatical modifier|qualifier]], [[rebuttal]], and backing. The initial claim of an argument is the assertion that the arguer is trying to confirm to another member in an argument. The grounds of an argument are the evidence to support the initial assertion. The warrant are the assumptions that are being used to connect the grounds to the claim. Backing is any additional supporting evidence to prove a claim and to support the warrant. Qualifiers are used to show that a claim may not always be correct (such as: sometimes, rather, somewhat) to show that the claim may not always apply to every situation. Finally, a rebuttal provides another member in a discussion to propose another valid claim for the argument.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Lab|first=Purdue Writing|title=Toulmin Argument|url=https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/academic_writing/historical_perspectives_on_argumentation/toulmin_argument.html|access-date=2020-11-19|website=Purdue Writing Lab|language=en|archive-date=20 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201120163103/https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/academic_writing/historical_perspectives_on_argumentation/toulmin_argument.html|url-status=live}}</ref>{{relevance inline|date=May 2025}}

In an appeal to the stone, there is only grounds and claims without providing valid warrants or backing to substantiate their claim. Furthermore, appeals to the stone typically do not use qualifiers, limiting the scope of a rebuttal. Without providing valid evidence in an appeal to the stone, it is difficult to provide a rebuttal to the claim.{{citation needed|date=May 2022}}

==Similar theories==
{{original research section|date=April 2025}}

===Reductio ad absurdum===
{{failed verification span|Appeal to the stone shares similarities in structure to ''[[reductio ad absurdum]]''|date=May 2025}} (Latin for “reduction to absurdity”) which states that an argument's assumptions or methods will lead to absurd conclusions.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Odintsov|first=S. P.|date=2003-11-23|title="Reductio ad absurdum" and Łukasiewicz's modalities|journal=Logic and Logical Philosophy|volume=11|doi=10.12775/llp.2003.008|issn=1425-3305|doi-access=free}}</ref> Although appeal to the stone does not explicitly state that an initial statement is absurd, a rejection of the initial claim often times presumes that the initial claim is incorrect or absurd. ''Reductio ad absurdum'' makes the assertion that if an initial claim is true, then some other absurd conclusion must also be true.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Rescher|first=Nicholas|date=2017|title=Reductio ad absurdum|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.24894/hwph.3487|access-date=2020-11-19|website=Historisches Wörterbuch der Philosophie online|doi=10.24894/hwph.3487|archive-date=7 October 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231007223258/https://www.schwabeonline.ch/schwabe-xaveropp/elibrary/start.xav?qn=%24%24%24OpenURL%24%24%24&id=doi%3A10.24894%2FHWPh.3487#__elibrary__%2F%2F*%5B%40attr_id%3D%27verw.reductio.ad.absurdum%27%5D__1696717997090|url-status=live|url-access=subscription}}</ref>{{relevance inline|date=May 2025}}

===Begging the question===
{{off topic|date=May 2025}}
[[Begging the question]], also called ''petitio principii'', is a conclusion based on an assumption that requires further proof or elaboration to be validated.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Garner|first=Bryan A.|date=2016|title=Garner's Modern English Usage|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1093/acref/9780190491482.001.0001|journal=Oxford Reference|doi=10.1093/acref/9780190491482.001.0001|isbn=978-0-19-049148-2|access-date=19 November 2020|archive-date=7 October 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231007223201/https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/acref/9780190491482.001.0001/acref-9780190491482|url-status=live|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Begging the question, is more formally synonymous with “ignoring a question under the assumption it has already been answered.” Begging the question often creates further questioning and colloquial use of this theory has been repurposed to mean “a question that begs to be answered”.<ref>{{Citation|last=Griffith|first=Bryant|chapter=What Does it Mean to Question?|date=2016|chapter-url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/978-94-6300-642-2_3|title=NextGeners|pages=53–83|place=Rotterdam|publisher=SensePublishers|doi=10.1007/978-94-6300-642-2_3|isbn=978-94-6300-642-2|access-date=2020-11-19|archive-date=7 October 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231007223158/https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-94-6300-642-2_3|url-status=live|chapter-url-access=subscription}}</ref>

=== Ad nauseam ===
''[[Ad nauseam]]'' is Latin and is associated with repeating something to a sickening or excessive degree. This fallacy can be used in arguments to by asserting an opinion on a subject matter to an excessive degree. In an appeal to the stone, with a lack of evidence to support a rejection of a claim, it can likely lead to an ''ad nauseam'' argument. If an argument with an appeal to the stone cannot be resolved, it will likely lead to both parties arguing until they are bored of the discussion and cannot come to a satisfactory conclusion.<ref>{{Cite web|title=AD NAUSEAM {{!}} meaning in the Cambridge English Dictionary|url=https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english/ad-nauseam|access-date=2020-11-20|website=dictionary.cambridge.org|language=en|archive-date=2 June 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200602091351/https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english/ad-nauseam|url-status=live}}</ref>{{failed verification|date=May 2025}}

=== Denialism ===
{{off topic|date=May 2025}}
[[Denialism]] is a rejection of facts and reality even when there is strong evidence.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Definition of DENIALISM|url=https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/denialism|access-date=2020-11-20|website=www.merriam-webster.com|language=en|archive-date=28 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201128092905/https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/denialism|url-status=live}}</ref> Those using denialism are likely using it with ulterior motives such as self-interests or to avoid an uncomfortable truth. The most common way to rebut a denial is through debunking by dissecting the root of the belief and providing evidence to disprove their idea, point by point.
